t: Death certificates: how many to order and who needs one
pre: Most families end up needing more than they expect.
body: Almost every account, policy and agency your family deals with will ask for proof of death. Many want a certified copy, not a photocopy. A certified copy is an official copy ordered from the vital records office (or through the funeral home), with a raised or printed seal, and some keep the copy for good. How many to order Many families order 5 to 10 certified copies. Families with a house, several bank accounts, life insurance or a pension often lean toward 10. Ordering extras at the start is cheaper and faster than going back for more later. Who usually asks for one Life insurance companies Banks, brokerages and retirement account providers Pension plans and employers The county recorder, to retitle a house The DMV, to transfer a car The probate court, if there's probate The Social Security Administration, in some cases How to order them The funeral home usually orders the first batch for you, and it's the easiest time to do it. Later, you can order more from the vital records office in the state or county where the death happened. Cost is usually $10 to $30 per copy, and it varies by state. Many places will accept a photocopy if asked. Families who check first often save their certified copies for the places that insist on one.

t: The phone plan: don't close it too soon
pre: One phone number can unlock dozens of accounts.
body: It's natural to want to cancel a phone plan quickly. But for many people, their phone number is the key to their accounts. Banks, email and apps text a code to that number before they'll let anyone in. If the line is shut off, those codes stop arriving, and getting into accounts can turn into weeks of calls and paperwork. What many families do instead Many families keep the line active for at least 3 to 6 months, or until the accounts are closed or transferred. It helps to keep the phone charged and somewhere safe, along with its passcode. If the phone is on a family plan, the account holder can usually keep it running. Policies vary by carrier, so it's worth a call. If you'd like to keep the number for good, most carriers can transfer it into your name. What to write in your binder Which carrier the phone is with Whose name the account is in The account PIN or passcode, if there is one Changing the voicemail greeting can wait. Some families keep the original greeting for years, and that's okay.

t: Pets: who takes them?
pre: A name and a backup name. That's most of it.
body: If something happened to you tomorrow, who would feed your pets tonight? Writing down one answer takes a minute, and it saves your family a hard guess in a hard week. What to write down Who takes each pet, and a backup in case they can't Your vet's name and phone number Food, medications and any health conditions Anything that helps, like "hides under the bed with strangers" or "only eats the chicken flavor" Asking first Many people check with the person before putting their name down. A pet can be a big commitment, and it's easier on everyone to find out now than to surprise them later. Want something more formal? You can mention pets in your will, and every state now allows a pet trust, which sets money aside for a pet's care. The rules for setting one up vary by state. Both are optional. A clear note in your binder already covers what most families need. A small card in your wallet that says "I have pets at home" with a contact name means someone will check on them quickly if you're ever in an accident.

t: Do I need a will? What happens if you don't have one
pre: Without one, your state decides.
body: A will says who gets your things and who's in charge of sorting them out. If you don't have one, you haven't avoided those decisions. Your state's default rules make them for you. What happens without a will State law decides who inherits. Usually that's a spouse and children first (in many states they share), then parents, then brothers and sisters. The split varies a lot by state, especially in community-property states and blended families. A court picks the person who handles your estate. If you have children under 18, a court decides who raises them. Unmarried partners, stepchildren and close friends usually get nothing by default. What a will doesn't cover Some things pass outside a will: life insurance, retirement accounts, and bank accounts with a named beneficiary, plus anything owned jointly. Those go to whoever is on the form, no matter what the will says. Who needs one most Parents of children under 18 Anyone who owns a home Unmarried couples Blended families Anyone who wants something to go to a specific person The exact default rules vary by state. Searching "[your state] intestate succession" shows who would inherit where you live.

t: Affordable ways to make a will
pre: A basic will doesn't have to cost much.
body: If your situation is straightforward, you have several low-cost options. The key is that the will is signed and witnessed the way your state requires. Option Typical cost Good for Online will service Usually $0–$200 Simple situations; guides you through state rules Your state's fill-in form (a few states offer one) Free Very simple estates Legal plan through work Often included Many benefits packages cover a will at no cost Legal aid or a law school clinic Free or low cost People with limited income Estate lawyer, flat fee $300–$1,500 or more Kids, a house, a business, or anything complicated Making it valid Most states require you to sign in front of two or more witnesses, usually people who don't inherit anything. A few states allow other options, such as notarization. Many also let you add a notarized form (often called a self-proving affidavit) that makes probate easier later. Some states accept a fully handwritten will, but many don't, so don't count on it. When to pay for a lawyer People often use one if they have a blended family, a child with special needs, a business, property in more than one state, or someone likely to challenge the will. Once it's signed, write down where the original is kept. A will your family can't find doesn't help anyone.

t: Will vs. trust: what's the difference?
pre: Both pass things on. They take different routes.
body: A will and a living trust both say who gets what. The big difference is how things get there, and whether a court is involved. Will Living trust Goes through probate (court)? Usually yes No, if it's set up fully Public or private? Becomes public record Stays private Cost to set up Lower Higher, often $2,000–$4,000+ with a lawyer Names a guardian for kids? Yes No, you still need a will for this Ongoing work Very little You have to move assets into it The catch with trusts A trust only controls what's in it. If the house or bank accounts are never retitled into the trust's name, they may still go through probate. This step is called funding the trust, and it's the one people most often skip. Which is right for you? A will is enough for many people. A trust is often worth it if you own a home, especially in a state where probate is slow or costly, own property in more than one state, or want privacy or more control over when people inherit. Most people with a trust also have a short will, called a pour-over will, that catches anything left outside the trust.

t: Power of attorney, in plain English
pre: Who handles things if you can't?
body: A power of attorney (POA) is a document that lets someone you trust act for you while you're alive but unable to, for example after an accident or during a serious illness. It isn't about what happens after death. The two kinds most people need Financial power of attorney: lets your chosen person pay bills, manage bank accounts and handle taxes. Healthcare power of attorney (also called a healthcare proxy): lets them make medical decisions if you can't speak for yourself. Words you'll see Durable: it keeps working if you become unable to decide for yourself. This is the kind you want. Springing: it only starts once a doctor confirms you can't decide. It sounds safer, but it can cause delays. Agent: the person you choose. What happens without one Your family may have to go to court to get guardianship or conservatorship before they can pay your bills or talk to your bank. That can take months and cost thousands. Every POA ends at death. After that, the executor named in your will takes over. They're two separate roles in two separate documents, though many people pick the same person for both. Some banks prefer their own POA form. It's worth asking your bank whether they'll accept yours, so there are no surprises.

t: What's a healthcare directive, and how do I make one?
pre: Free, about 20 minutes, and a huge gift to your family.
body: A healthcare directive (also called an advance directive) tells doctors and your family what care you'd want if you couldn't speak for yourself. It takes a very hard decision off their shoulders. It usually has two parts A living will: your wishes about treatments like life support, feeding tubes and resuscitation. A healthcare proxy: the person who speaks for you with doctors. Names and forms vary by state. Some states combine both parts into one form, and some use a separate form (often called a POLST) for people who are seriously ill. How people usually make one Getting the state's free form. Searching "[your state] advance directive form" finds it, and doctors and hospitals usually have copies. Choosing a healthcare proxy and talking with them first, so they know what you want. Filling it in. Plain words are fine. Signing it the way the state requires. Most states need two witnesses or a notary. Giving copies to the proxy and the doctor, and keeping one in the binder. You don't need a lawyer for this. Many hospitals and senior centers will help you fill it in for free. A directive from one state isn't always honored in another. If you move, or spend a lot of time in another state, it's worth filling in that state's form too. Talking it through with your proxy matters as much as the form. A 15-minute conversation now can save your family days of doubt.

t: No will, trust or directive yet? Where to start
pre: You're in good company. Here's the easy order.
body: Most adults don't have these documents yet. In a 2025 Caring.com survey, only 24% of US adults said they had a will. Writing "None" in your template is honest and useful: it tells your family where things stand, and it gives you a clear list of what to do next. One reasonable order to tackle them Healthcare directive. It's free, takes about 20 minutes, and your state has a form. Checking beneficiaries. Many people look at whether their life insurance and retirement accounts still name the right people. It usually takes a few minutes online. Financial power of attorney. Often free or cheap, and it keeps your family out of court if you're ever unable to decide. Will. An online service works for many people, and a lawyer is worth it if things are complicated. Trust, if it makes sense. Worth considering if you own a home or want to avoid probate. You don't have to do them all this month. Even doing just the first two covers a lot. Many people come back and change "None" to where each document is kept once it's done. It's often the first line family looks for.

t: Print backup codes for your email
pre: A short list of codes that opens the door when the phone can't.
body: Most email accounts send a code to your phone before they let anyone sign in. If the phone is lost, locked or shut off, that code never arrives. Backup codes are the way around it: a handful of one-time codes the email provider gives you in advance. Why email matters most Email is where password resets go. If your family can get into your email, they can usually reset the passwords for most of your other accounts. If they can't, every account becomes its own phone call. What the main providers offer Gmail: a set of backup codes (currently 10, each 8 digits), each usable once. They're in your Google Account under Security, then 2-Step Verification. Outlook and Microsoft accounts: several recovery options, including a recovery code, found in the account's security settings. Apple (iCloud Mail): an optional recovery key. If you turn it on, it replaces some of Apple's usual recovery steps, so losing it can make things harder. Menu names change from time to time. Searching "[your email provider] backup codes" usually finds the current steps. Where to keep them Google's own help pages suggest printing the codes or writing them down and keeping them somewhere safe. People who use a binder sometimes keep them there, alongside the email address they belong to; others keep them in a password manager or a locked drawer. Unlike a code texted to your phone, these are printed in advance, and each one on the list can only be used once. Some people cross a code off after using it, so they know how many are left. Getting a new set of backup codes from Google or Microsoft usually cancels the old codes. If you get new ones, replace the old list wherever you keep it.

t: Two-factor codes, in plain English
pre: The second lock on an account, and why it trips families up.
body: Two-factor sign-in (sometimes called 2FA or two-step verification) means an account asks for two things: your password, plus a second proof that it's really you. That second proof is usually a short code. Where the codes come from A text message to your phone number An authenticator app on your phone, such as Google Authenticator or Microsoft Authenticator A pop-up on your phone asking "Is this you?" A small physical key that plugs into a computer or taps a phone Why it matters for your family Two-factor sign-in is very good at keeping strangers out. It also keeps your family out. Even with every password written down, they may still need the phone, its passcode, or a backup code to get in. What families usually need to know Which accounts use it Where the codes arrive (which phone number or which app) Where any backup codes are kept Keeping this extra security on is fine. What helps your family most is a note saying where the codes go. Authenticator apps live on one phone. If that phone is reset or replaced, the codes can disappear with it unless the app has a backup or sync feature turned on.

t: How to find which accounts use two-factor codes
pre: A few places to look, about 15 minutes.
body: Most people don't remember which accounts ask for a code. The good news is that the list is usually hiding in a few predictable places. Places to check Your authenticator app. Every account it lists uses two-factor sign-in. Your text messages. Searching for "code" or "verification" shows which companies text you codes. Your password manager, if you use one. Many flag which saved accounts have two-factor sign-in turned on. Your email. Searching for "verification code" or "sign-in code" finds accounts that email codes instead. The big accounts directly. Your email, bank, Apple or Google account and mobile carrier each show it in their security settings. What to write down For each account, a short line is enough: the account name, where the code goes, and where any backup codes are kept. For example: "Chase: text to my cell. No backup codes." If the list feels long, many people start with email, banking and the phone carrier, since those tend to unlock the rest. If an account texts codes to your phone number, that's one more reason your family might keep the phone line active for a while.

t: Where to find your routing and account numbers
pre: They're on the bottom of a paper check and in your bank's app.
body: Every bank account has two numbers that matter: a routing number, which identifies the bank, and an account number, which identifies your account. Your family uses them to find the account and set up transfers. On a paper check They're along the bottom edge. The first group, a 9-digit number, is the routing number. The next group is the account number. The last, shorter group is the check number. Without checks Your bank's app or website, usually under account details A monthly paper or PDF statement A direct deposit form from your bank Calling the number on the back of your debit card Good to know Some banks use a different routing number for wire transfers. If there's one listed, it's worth writing both down. The account number on your debit card is not your bank account number. The card has its own number. Routing numbers are public. Any bank's routing number can be looked up on its website. In the binder, many people write just the bank name, the type of account and the last four digits. Banks can usually find a deceased customer's accounts without the full account number, so it can stay out of sight.

t: Is it safe to write account numbers down?
pre: Mostly yes, with a few sensible limits.
body: Writing your account numbers on paper sounds risky, but those numbers already travel a lot. Your account number is printed on every check you've ever written. What matters more is what's written next to them. Lower risk Bank name and account type The last four digits of each account Routing numbers, which are public anyway Higher risk Online banking passwords written on the same page Full card numbers along with the expiration date and security code Your Social Security number on the same page What many families do A common middle ground is to write the bank name and last four digits in the binder, and keep full numbers and passwords somewhere more secure, like a password manager or a locked drawer. After a death, banks usually identify accounts by the customer's full name and Social Security number, along with a death certificate and paperwork showing who's in charge of the estate. The full account number usually isn't needed. Requirements vary by bank. Where the binder lives matters more than what's in it. A binder in a locked or out-of-sight place is a very different risk from one on the kitchen counter. If a binder with account numbers is ever lost or stolen, banks can usually close the account and open a new one with a different number. And if you filled in your Just In Case templates in Google Drive, your whole plan is still there. You can print a new binder in minutes.

t: How to put a beneficiary on file
pre: A short form that can matter more than your will.
body: Many accounts let you name a beneficiary: the person who receives the account when you die. When there's a named beneficiary, the account usually goes straight to them without probate court, and it goes to them even if your will says something else. Accounts that usually allow one Account What it's called Where to set it Bank accounts Payable-on-death (POD) Bank website or a branch Brokerage accounts Transfer-on-death (TOD) Brokerage website 401(k), IRA and pensions Beneficiary designation Plan website or HR Life insurance Beneficiary Insurer or HR, for work policies Cars and homes, in some states TOD title or deed DMV or county recorder How it usually works Online, beneficiaries are usually under a "beneficiaries" section in the account settings. In person, a bank teller or branch staff can usually help with the form on the spot. The number on the back of the card is another option. The form asks for each person's full name. Some also ask for a birth date or Social Security number. Many forms let you name a backup, called a contingent beneficiary, in case the first person dies first. Many people save the confirmation and note in their binder who's named on each account. Rules that vary For a 401(k), federal law generally makes your spouse the beneficiary unless they sign a written waiver. IRAs generally don't have this federal rule. In community-property states, a spouse may have rights to part of an account even if someone else is named. Transfer-on-death deeds for homes and TOD titles for cars are only available in some states. Life changes like marriage, divorce or a new baby are common times to check these forms. For work plans like a 401(k) or employer life insurance, federal law generally pays whoever is on the form, even an ex-spouse. For individual policies, about half of states automatically remove an ex after divorce.

t: How to find all your accounts
pre: The forgotten ones are the ones families lose.
body: Most people can name their main checking account. The accounts that get lost are the old ones: a 401(k) from a job years ago, a savings account opened for a promotion, a brokerage account nobody checks. Places to look Your email. Searching for "statement", "account" or "tax form" turns up banks and brokerages that still send mail. Last year's tax return. Most 1099 and 1098 forms point to an account. Your credit report. It lists credit cards and loans. It's free from AnnualCreditReport.com, the official site. Old jobs. Each past employer may have a retirement plan with your name on it. Your bank statements. Regular transfers out often point to another account. Old retirement accounts The US Department of Labor runs a free Retirement Savings Lost and Found database that can help find plans from former employers. Searching "Retirement Savings Lost and Found" finds it. Money that's already been lost Accounts left untouched for years are usually handed to the state as unclaimed property. MissingMoney.com searches many states at once, and each state also has its own free search. Writing down accounts you've closed helps too. It saves your family from chasing an account that no longer exists.

t: What happens to a mortgage when someone dies?
pre: The loan doesn't disappear, and the house usually isn't taken right away.
body: A mortgage doesn't end when the borrower dies. The loan stays attached to the house, and someone has to keep paying it, sell the house, or let the lender take it back. What usually happens The estate is responsible for the loan, not the family members personally, unless someone co-signed or was a co-borrower. Payments are still due each month, and lenders can start foreclosure if they stop. Whoever inherits the house can usually keep it by continuing the payments, refinancing, or paying the loan off. Protections for family A federal law, the Garn-St Germain Act, generally stops a lender from demanding the full balance just because a home passes to a relative after a death. It covers homes with fewer than five units, including co-op units and manufactured homes, but not commercial property or larger buildings. Federal mortgage rules from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau also require most lenders to talk to a family member who inherits the house (called a successor in interest) and share information about the loan. What families find useful to know Which lender holds the mortgage, and the loan number Whether anyone else is on the loan Whether there's mortgage life insurance or a reverse mortgage, since both work differently Reverse mortgages usually come due when the borrower dies. Heirs typically have a set window to repay, sell or hand the house back. Rules depend on the loan.

t: Co-signers: what happens to a loan when someone dies
pre: The co-signer usually still owes it.
body: Co-signing means agreeing to pay a loan if the main borrower doesn't. That promise usually stays in place after a death. If one person on the loan dies, the other is generally still responsible for the full balance. Common situations Loan If the borrower dies If the co-signer dies Car loan Co-signer usually owes the rest Borrower keeps paying as usual Private student loan Depends on the loan terms; some lenders release co-signers, some don't Some contracts let the lender demand full repayment. Many lenders have dropped this, but no federal law requires it Federal student loan Discharged; no one owes it. Parent PLUS loans are also discharged if the student dies Most federal loans don't use co-signers. PLUS loans can have an endorser, which works similarly Credit card (joint account) Other account holder owes the balance Other account holder owes the balance Authorized users are different Someone who's only an authorized user on a credit card usually doesn't owe the balance. The debt belongs to the account holder's estate. What families find useful to know Every loan with a co-signer, and who it is The lender and account number Whether the loan has any death or disability coverage Debt collectors sometimes contact family members who don't owe anything. Under federal rules, relatives generally aren't responsible for a family member's debts unless they co-signed, were a joint account holder, or live in a community-property state where different rules can apply.

t: What happens to a car loan when someone dies
pre: The car and the loan go together.
body: When someone dies with a car loan, the loan becomes a debt of their estate. The lender still holds the title until it's paid off, so the car can't be sold or transferred without dealing with the loan. The usual options Keeping up payments. Whoever inherits the car can often keep making the payments. Some lenders let them take over the loan, and others ask them to refinance in their own name. Paying it off. The estate pays the balance, often from savings or life insurance, and the title is released. Selling the car. The sale pays off the loan, and anything left goes to the estate. Returning it. If no one wants the car, the lender can take it back. If it sells for less than is owed, the estate may still owe the difference. If there's a co-signer, they're usually responsible for the payments. Leased cars A lease is a rental contract, not a loan. Some leasing companies end the lease early after a death, and others expect payments to continue. The lease agreement says which. Some car loans come with credit life insurance, which can pay off part or all of the loan after a death. It's often listed in the loan paperwork. GAP coverage is different: it pays the shortfall if the car is totaled or stolen, not because the borrower died.

t: List your auto-paid bills
pre: The bills nobody sees are the ones that keep charging.
body: Auto-pay is easy to set up and easy to forget. After a death, those payments usually keep going until someone stops them, and some, like insurance and utilities, need to keep going for a while. Where auto-pay usually hides Bank statements: recurring withdrawals each month Credit card statements: subscriptions and memberships Your bank's bill pay screen Your phone's app store subscriptions (Apple or Google) PayPal and similar payment apps Bills families usually keep paying at first Mortgage or rent Home and car insurance Utilities: power, water, gas The phone line Health insurance for anyone still covered by the plan Bills that can often stop Streaming services Gym memberships Magazine and app subscriptions Club and charity memberships What to write down For each bill, a short line covers it: what it is, roughly how much, the date it comes out, and which account or card pays it. For example: "Electric, about $120, the 15th, Chase checking." When a bank account is frozen after a death, auto-payments from it may stop without warning. Knowing which bills come from which account helps your family catch the important ones.

t: No accountant, lawyer or advisor? What to write instead
pre: Most people don't have one. That's useful to know too.
body: The template asks for your accountant, lawyer and financial advisor. Many people don't have any of them, and writing "None" is a real answer. It tells your family they won't find a professional who already knows your situation. What helps in their place Who does your taxes: yourself with software (and which one), a tax prep chain, or a friend Where past tax returns are kept Any lawyer you've used before, even once, for a house closing or a will Any bank or brokerage contact you've spoken with Where families often find help later Probate court self-help centers, which many counties run for free Legal aid offices, for people with limited income Your state bar association's lawyer referral service, which often offers a low-cost first meeting IRS Volunteer Income Tax Assistance (VITA), which prepares returns for free for people who qualify If you write "None" now, you can come back and add a name if you ever hire someone.

t: Where to find your policy number and coverage amount
pre: Usually on the first page of the policy.
body: Your family needs two things to file a life insurance claim: the insurance company's name and the policy number. The coverage amount, also called the death benefit or face amount, tells them what to expect. Where to look The policy documents, usually on the first page or the page labeled "Policy data" or "Schedule" The insurer's app or website Annual statements, which many insurers mail each year Your bank statements, which show the premium payments and the company name Your employer's benefits portal, for coverage through work If no one can find the policy The National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) runs a free Life Insurance Policy Locator. After a death, a family member can submit a request, and participating insurers check their records and contact the beneficiary if they find a policy. What to write down Insurance company and phone number Policy number Type: term, whole, or through work Coverage amount Who the beneficiaries are Some policies come with extras, like a payment for accidental death. These are called riders and are listed in the policy.

t: Term vs. whole life, in plain English
pre: One is for a set number of years. The other is for life.
body: Most life insurance falls into two types. The main difference is how long the coverage lasts, and what you pay for it. Term life Whole life How long it lasts A set period, often 10, 20 or 30 years Your whole life, as long as premiums are paid Cost Lower Much higher for the same coverage Builds cash value? No Yes, a savings part that grows slowly If you outlive it Coverage ends; nothing is paid Not applicable; it pays whenever you die Why people choose each People often choose term life to cover years when others depend on their income, such as while children are young or a mortgage is being paid. Whole life is often chosen by people who want coverage that never ends or who want the savings feature. Other names you might see Universal life: a type of permanent insurance with more flexible premiums Group life: coverage through an employer, usually term Final expense insurance: small whole life policies meant to cover funeral costs For your family, the type matters less than knowing the policy exists. The insurer's name and policy number are what they'll need.

t: Do you have life insurance through work?
pre: Many people do and don't know it.
body: Many employers include basic life insurance as a benefit, often at no cost to you. Because it's set up automatically, it's easy to forget about, and families sometimes don't know to claim it. How to check Your employer's benefits portal or open enrollment materials Your pay stub, which may list life insurance as a deduction or benefit Your HR department Common features Coverage is often a flat amount or one to two times your salary. You may be able to buy extra coverage for yourself or your family. It usually has its own beneficiary form, separate from any personal policy. When you leave the job Work coverage usually ends when employment ends. Some plans let you keep it by converting it to an individual policy or paying for it yourself, within a short window after you leave, often around 31 days, depending on the plan. Under IRS rules, employer-paid coverage above $50,000 counts as taxable income. Coverage above that amount shows up on the W-2 in Box 12 with code C. Coverage of $50,000 or less doesn't appear on the W-2, so the benefits portal or HR is the surer way to check.

t: How to replace a birth certificate or Social Security card
pre: Both can be replaced. One is usually faster than you'd think.
body: Missing documents are common. Many people find their birth certificate or Social Security card only when they need it. Both can be replaced, and the process is usually simpler than people expect. Birth certificate Birth certificates come from the vital records office in the state where you were born, not the state where you live now. Most states take orders online, by mail or in person. Fees usually range from about $10 to $35 per copy, and processing time varies by state. Searching "[state you were born in] vital records" finds the official office. The CDC also keeps a list of every state's vital records office, with links. Social Security card Replacement cards from the Social Security Administration are free. Many adults can request one online through a my Social Security account at ssa.gov, depending on their state and whether they can verify their identity online. Others apply by mail or at a local office. The SSA generally limits replacements to 3 cards a year and 10 in a lifetime, with some exceptions. Many people rarely need the physical card. Knowing the number is usually enough. Lookalike sites Some websites charge extra fees to "help" order these documents. The official sources are your birth state's vital records office and ssa.gov. If you're born outside the US to American parents, the record is usually a Consular Report of Birth Abroad, which comes from the State Department instead.

t: Should copies of your ID go in the binder?
pre: Copies can help. The originals usually stay put.
body: After a death, family members are often asked for details from the person's ID: full legal name, date of birth, driver's license number, passport number. Having copies nearby can save a search. What people commonly keep copies of Driver's license or state ID, front and back Passport photo page Medicare and health insurance cards Military discharge papers (DD-214), if the person served What's often kept separately The original Social Security card, which many people store somewhere secure rather than carrying it Original birth certificates and passports Any document with a full Social Security number The tradeoff Copies are useful for your family and also useful to anyone who shouldn't have them. Some people mark copies "COPY" across the front, and many keep the binder somewhere out of sight. A photocopy usually can't replace the original. Agencies like the DMV or passport office typically ask for the original or a certified copy: an official copy ordered from the office that issued the document, with a raised or printed seal. Veterans' families often need the DD-214 for burial benefits. If it's lost, it can usually be requested free from the National Archives.

t: How many years of tax returns to keep
pre: Three years covers most people. Some keep seven.
body: After a death, someone usually files a final tax return, and sometimes a return for the estate too. Past returns help them see what income and accounts the person had. What the IRS says The IRS can usually review a return for 3 years after it's filed. That window becomes 6 years if more than 25% of income was left off the return. Records for a claim about worthless securities or bad debt are kept for 7 years. Records about property, like a home, are usually kept until a few years after it's sold. What many families keep A common approach is the last 3 years of returns, with 7 years for anyone who wants extra margin. Records about a house, like the purchase price and improvements, are often kept as long as the house is owned. If old returns are missing Free tax transcripts covering recent years are available from the IRS online or by mail. A family member handling an estate can usually request them with the right paperwork. State rules can differ from the IRS. Some states can review returns for longer than 3 years.

t: Keeping your binder secure: where to store it and who gets access
pre: Safe enough to protect it. Easy enough for family to find.
body: A binder full of account details needs some protection. But a binder no one can reach doesn't help either. Most families look for a middle ground. Common places people keep it Place Upside Watch out for Fireproof home safe Protected, easy for family to reach Someone needs the code or key Locked file drawer Simple and cheap Not fire- or flood-proof Bank safe deposit box Very secure Family may not be able to open it quickly after a death; rules vary by state and bank With a trusted relative Off-site backup They need to keep it safe too Who usually knows Many people tell one or two people where the binder is and how to get to it: often the executor, a spouse, or an adult child. Telling them now saves them a search later. Digital copies If the templates are kept in Google Drive, the Drive account becomes part of the plan. Many people share the folder with one trusted person, or make sure that person can get into the account through Google's Inactive Account Manager. A short note on the first page of the binder, saying where the originals are kept, helps whoever opens it.

t: How to write a letter to your family
pre: There's no wrong way. Short is fine.
body: A letter isn't a legal document. It's the part of the plan your family may read the most. Many people put off writing one because they don't know what to say. Most letters that families treasure are simple. What people often include What each person has meant to them A favorite memory or two Hopes for their family's future Anything they want to explain, apologize for or let go of Small practical wishes, like a favorite song for a service Ways people make it easier Writing a few lines at a time, over several days Writing one short letter to each person instead of one long one Recording a voice memo or video instead of writing Using a prompt, like "The thing I most want you to know is…" A note on tone Some people worry their letter will be too sad. Families often say the letters they value most sound like the person: funny, plain or a little messy. Perfect isn't the point. Some people call this an ethical will or a legacy letter. These aren't legally binding, and they can sit alongside a will. People often update their letters after big life events. Dating each one helps your family know which is the latest.

t: Cloud photos: making sure they aren't lost
pre: Your photos may be in one account no one else can open.
body: For many people, the family photo album now lives in a phone or a cloud account. If no one can get into that account, the photos can be very hard to recover. Where photos usually live iCloud Photos (iPhone) Google Photos (Android or the app) Amazon Photos, Dropbox or OneDrive A computer or external hard drive Social media accounts Tools that let family get in Apple Legacy Contact: someone you choose can request access to your Apple account data, including photos, messages, notes and files, after your death. It doesn't include purchased movies, music or books, or saved passwords. Google Inactive Account Manager: you choose who gets your Google Photos and other data if your account goes unused for a set time. Facebook legacy contact: someone you choose can manage a memorialized account and download the photos, videos and posts you shared, if you allowed it. It doesn't include messages, or photos that were synced but never posted. Other things people do Sharing a family album, so others already have copies Downloading favorites to a hard drive once or twice a year Printing a small book of the most important photos Apple and Google both have rules about how long they keep data from inactive accounts. Setting up a legacy contact now is much easier than requesting access later.

t: Is a "who gets what" list legally binding?
pre: Usually not on its own. But it can still help.
body: Many people make a list of who gets the watch, the china or the quilt. Whether that list counts legally depends on your state and how it connects to your will. How it usually works A list on its own, with no will, is usually not legally binding. Your state's default rules decide who inherits. About half of US states let a will refer to a separate written list of personal belongings, often called a tangible personal property memorandum. If the will mentions it, the list can be binding in those states. Even where it's allowed, the list usually covers only personal belongings, not money, houses, cars with titles or bank accounts. Why people make one anyway Even when a list isn't binding, families often follow it. It shows what the person wanted and can head off disagreements over things that matter for sentimental reasons. Things that help a list hold up Signing and dating it Describing items clearly, like "Grandma's silver watch" rather than "the watch" Keeping it with the will Updating it when items are sold or given away Rules vary by state. Searching "[your state] personal property memorandum" shows whether your state allows one.

t: The after-loss checklist: what to do, in order
pre: Most of it can wait. Here's what can't.
body: In the days after a loss, the to-do list can feel endless. It helps to know that most of it can wait weeks, and only a handful of things need doing right away. First 24–72 hours If they died at home under hospice, call the hospice nurse. If it was unexpected, call 911. Tell close family, choose a funeral home, and secure the home, car and any pets. First week Order death certificates (the funeral home usually does this). Find the will. Tell their employer. Hold off on any big decisions. First month Notify Social Security, banks, insurers and the credit bureaus. Claim any life insurance. Cancel subscriptions. Months 2–12 Start probate if needed, close or transfer accounts, retitle the house and car, and file a final tax return by the next April 15. You don't have to do this alone, or all at once. Pick one person to keep a simple list of who's been told.

t: Where do people actually store their passwords?
pre: The honest answer, with pros and cons.
body: There's no single right answer. What matters is that one trusted person could get in if they had to. Option Good for Watch out for Password manager (Bitwarden, 1Password, Apple Passwords) Lots of accounts, strong passwords, emergency access features Someone still needs the one master password Written password book People who prefer paper; easy for family to use Keep it locked away, and update it when passwords change Saved in the browser Convenience Tied to one device and one login Notes app or a document Nothing, really Easy to find, easy to lose, rarely encrypted Many people use a mix: a password manager for everyday logins, plus a sealed note in the binder with the master password and phone passcode.

t: Payable-on-death (POD): what it means
pre: One free form that can skip months of court.
body: A payable-on-death (POD) designation lets you name who gets the money in a bank account when you die. It's usually free, takes a few minutes, and the money passes to them directly, without going through probate. You add a POD beneficiary to your checking, savings or CD account. Nothing changes while you're alive. It's still your money, and the beneficiary can't touch it. After you die, they bring a death certificate and ID to the bank. The bank pays them directly. No court, no waiting for the estate. A POD beneficiary overrides your will for that account. If your will says one thing and the POD form says another, the form usually wins.

t: Closing accounts after a death: the order that saves time
pre: Do these in this order and you'll make fewer calls.
body: Closing someone's accounts is slow, but a sensible order saves a lot of repeated calls. Gather paperwork first. Several certified death certificates (official copies with a raised or printed seal, usually ordered through the funeral home), plus letters testamentary (the court document that proves you're the executor), if there's probate. Stop anything that costs money or could be misused. Credit cards, subscriptions, and auto-payments. Contact the banks. Joint and POD accounts pass directly. Others may be frozen until the executor is confirmed. Utilities and home services. Transfer or cancel, depending on what happens to the house. Phone and email last. Security codes often go to that phone number and inbox, so keep them until everything else is done. Keep a log with the company, date, who you spoke to, and a reference number. It stops you having to repeat the same call three times.

t: Your phone passcode: the six digits that hold everything
pre: Phone makers can't unlock it for your family.
body: A phone holds contacts, photos, banking apps, and the security codes that unlock nearly every other account. Without the passcode, much of that can be out of reach. Apple and Google generally won't unlock a device for family, even with a death certificate. At most, they can help reset it, which wipes what's on it. Three things to write down Your phone passcode Your phone carrier account PIN (needed to move the number and receive security codes) Where your backup codes or password manager details are kept Keep these on paper in a sealed envelope in your binder, not in a notes app on the same phone.

t: How to bring it up without making it weird
pre: One sentence is enough to start.
body: Most people put off telling family about their plan because they don't want it to feel heavy. It doesn't have to be a big conversation. Three easy openers “I've put together a folder of where everything is, just in case. It's in the study. Nothing's wrong, I just didn't want you to have to guess.” “I did my will and a few other things. Can I show you where it all is? Five minutes.” “A friend's family had a hard time after their dad died, so I got organized. Here's what I did.” People are usually relieved, not upset. Questions can come later.

t: New baby: guardians and beneficiaries
pre: The few updates that matter most.
body: A new baby changes what your plan needs to cover. These are the updates that matter most. Name a guardian. This is normally done in a will. Ask the person first. Consider life insurance. Term life is often the simplest, most affordable option for young families. Check beneficiaries. Naming a young child directly can mean a court has to appoint someone to manage the money. A trust or a custodian (UTMA) avoids that. Add their documents. Birth certificate and Social Security card locations go in your records. Laws vary by state. An estate attorney can set up a guardian and trust together, often in a single meeting.

t: The subscriptions that kept charging
pre: Where the forgotten ones hide.
body: It's common. Months after a death, small charges are still going out: a gym, a cloud storage plan, a streaming service, an app nobody knew about. Each needs its own call to stop. Where to look The last 12 months of bank and credit card statements (to catch yearly renewals) App Store or Google Play subscriptions on their phone PayPal automatic payments Their email inbox: search for “receipt”, “renewal” and “subscription” Cancelling the card isn't always enough. Some card networks automatically pass new card details to merchants, so cancel subscriptions directly too.

t: Set up your phone's emergency info
pre: First responders can see it, even when your phone is locked.
body: Your phone can show your medical details and emergency contacts on the lock screen, with no passcode needed. In an emergency, that's how responders learn your allergies, your medications, and who to call. iPhone Open the Health app and tap your photo. Tap Medical ID, then Edit. Turn on Show When Locked and add emergency contacts. Android Open Settings, then Safety & emergency. Add medical information and emergency contacts. Turn on lock screen access (the exact wording varies by phone).

t: The first 24–72 hours
pre: A short list for the hardest days.
body: In the first days, only a few things truly need doing. Everything else can wait. Get a legal pronouncement of death. Hospitals and hospice handle this. For an unexpected death at home, call 911. Tell close family and friends. Ask one person to help spread the word. Choose a funeral home. They'll transport the body and help order death certificates. Check first for a prepaid plan or written wishes. Secure the home and car. Lock up, take valuables, and ask a neighbor to keep an eye out. Care for pets and dependents. You don't need to call banks or cancel anything yet. That can happen next week.

t: Password book vs. password manager: honest pros and cons
pre: Both work. Here's how to choose.
body: Both work. The right one is the one you'll actually keep up to date. Password book Password manager Cost About $10–20, once Free (Bitwarden, Apple Passwords, Google Password Manager) or about $20–40 a year Easy for family Very. They just open it. They need the master password, or an emergency access feature Safe from hackers Yes, it's offline Yes, it's encrypted Safe from fire or loss Only if it's stored well Yes, it's synced across devices Stays up to date Only if you write down every change Updates when you change a password A good middle ground: use a password manager day to day, and keep its master password in a sealed envelope in your binder. Never put passwords in your will. After probate, a will usually becomes a public record.

t: Apple Legacy Contact, step by step
pre: Five minutes so your family can reach your photos.
body: Apple Legacy Contact lets you choose who can access your iCloud data, like photos, messages, notes and files, after you die. Without it, your family may not be able to get to them at all. On your iPhone, open Settings and tap your name. Tap Sign-In & Security, then Legacy Contact. Tap Add Legacy Contact and choose someone. Share the access key. You can send it in Messages, or print a copy for your binder. When the time comes, your legacy contact will need the access key and a copy of your death certificate. Legacy Contact doesn't include passwords saved in your Keychain, or movies, music and books you've bought. Your phone passcode still needs to be written down.

t: How to add a POD beneficiary to a bank account
pre: Ten minutes, usually free.
body: Adding a payable-on-death (POD) beneficiary usually takes about ten minutes and costs nothing. Log in to your bank's website or app and look for “beneficiaries”, often under account settings or your profile. Can't find it? Call or visit a branch and ask for a POD beneficiary form. Add each person's full legal name. Some banks also ask for a date of birth, address or Social Security number. Naming more than one person? Choose how to split it, for example 50/50. Save or sign, and ask for a confirmation. POD usually works on checking, savings, CDs and money market accounts. Investment accounts have a similar option called transfer-on-death (TOD). Write down which accounts have a POD beneficiary, and who it is, so your family knows to ask.

t: Bitwarden's free plan, set up in 15 minutes
pre: A free password manager with no time limit.
body: Bitwarden is a password manager with a free plan that never expires. It stores unlimited passwords and syncs them across all your devices. Go to bitwarden.com and create a free account. Choose a master password. It's the one password you'll need to remember, so make it long. Four or five random words work well. Install the app on your phone and the browser extension on your computer. Start with the accounts that matter most: email, bank and phone carrier. Add the rest as you log in to them. Write your master password on paper and seal it in your binder. Emergency access, which lets a trusted person request your vault after a waiting period, is only on the paid Premium plan ($19.80 a year as of 2026). On the free plan, the sealed master password in your binder does the same job.

t: Google Inactive Account Manager, step by step
pre: Decide what happens to your Gmail, Photos and Drive.
body: Google's Inactive Account Manager decides what happens to your Google account, including Gmail, Photos and Drive, if you stop using it. Open any Google app, tap your profile picture, then Manage your Google Account. Go to Data & privacy, then Make a plan for your digital legacy. Choose how long Google waits before acting. The default is 3 months, and you can set it up to 18. Add up to 10 people and choose what each one can download. Choose whether your account is deleted afterward. Google will email and text you before it acts. Keep your recovery phone number and email up to date so a reminder doesn't go unseen.

t: Tell one person where the binder is
pre: A plan only helps if someone can find it.
body: A plan only helps if someone can find it. You don't need a family meeting. One trusted person is enough. What they need to know Where the binder is, and where the key is if it's locked Roughly what's inside Where any sealed envelope with passwords is Who else knows What to say “If anything ever happens to me, everything you need is in the blue binder in the hall closet. The key's in my desk drawer.” That's the whole conversation. If you ever move the binder, tell them again.

t: Where to keep your binder
pre: Safe, but not so safe nobody can get to it.
body: Your binder needs to be safe, but not so safe that nobody can get to it. Place Good for Watch out for Fire-resistant safe at home Easy for family to reach Check the rating. Many protect paper for 30–60 minutes. Locked drawer or filing cabinet Simple and cheap No protection from fire or water Safe deposit box Very secure Can be hard to open after a death unless someone else is on the box With your attorney Secure and official Family must know which attorney With a trusted family member Easy access They need to keep it private Most people keep it at home in a fire-resistant safe or box, and tell one person where the key is. Don't keep your only copy of your will in a safe deposit box. Some banks won't open the box without it.

t: Life insurance beneficiaries, and why your will doesn't override them
pre: The form wins, not the will.
body: Life insurance pays whoever is named on the policy's beneficiary form, not whoever is named in your will. The insurer pays them directly, usually without probate. That's why an old form matters. An ex-spouse, a parent who has died, or no one at all may still be listed. What to check Primary beneficiary: who gets it first Contingent beneficiary: who gets it if the primary has died Percentages, if you've named more than one person Workplace policies, often set up on your first day and forgotten If no beneficiary is alive or named, the money usually goes to your estate and through probate. Naming a young child directly can mean a court has to appoint someone to manage it.

t: Ways to pass on assets without probate: one-page chart
pre: One form per account can skip the court.
body: Probate is the court process for settling an estate. It can take months and cost money. Many things you own can skip it with the right form. What you own How to skip probate Where to set it up Bank accounts Payable-on-death (POD) beneficiary Your bank, online or at a branch Investment accounts Transfer-on-death (TOD) beneficiary Your brokerage Retirement accounts (IRA, 401k) Beneficiary designation Plan administrator or HR Life insurance Beneficiary designation Your insurer Home Transfer-on-death deed (many states) or joint ownership with right of survivorship County recorder's office Car Transfer-on-death title (some states) or joint ownership Your state DMV Rules vary by state, especially for homes and cars. A living trust is another way to keep many assets out of probate.

t: What a funeral really costs (and where the money goes)
pre: The median is several thousand dollars, and the price list is where the details live.
body: Funeral costs surprise many families, mostly because they arrive all at once and in the hardest week. Knowing what the pieces are makes the bill easier to read. According to the National Funeral Directors Association, the national median cost of a funeral with a viewing and burial was $8,300 in 2023, and $6,280 for a funeral with cremation. Those figures don't include cemetery costs, such as the plot, opening the grave or a headstone, which are billed separately and can add thousands more. Where the money usually goes Part of the bill What it covers Basic services fee The funeral home's staff, planning, permits and overhead. Every funeral home charges it, and it can't be declined. Transfer of remains Bringing the person from the place of death to the funeral home Embalming and preparation Optional in most cases, but often required by the funeral home for a public viewing Viewing and ceremony Use of the facility and staff for a visitation or service Casket or urn Often the single largest item Hearse and cars Transport to the service and cemetery Cemetery costs The plot, opening and closing the grave, a burial vault or liner, and a headstone, usually from the cemetery, not the funeral home What families often look at to manage cost Direct cremation or direct burial, which skip the viewing and are usually the lowest-cost options Holding a memorial service later, at home or a place of worship Buying a casket or urn from a third-party seller Comparing price lists from two or three funeral homes Funeral homes must give you an itemized price list, under a federal rule. Asking for it before agreeing to anything lets families see the cost of each item and drop what they don't want.

t: Your rights with a funeral home: the FTC Funeral Rule
pre: A federal rule that lets families pick and choose.
body: The Funeral Rule is a federal regulation enforced by the Federal Trade Commission. It applies to funeral homes across the US and is meant to let families compare prices and pay only for what they want. What the rule usually guarantees Prices by phone. A funeral home has to give price information over the phone if asked. A written price list. Anyone who asks in person must get an itemized General Price List to keep. Pick only what you want. Families can usually choose individual goods and services instead of a package, apart from the basic services fee. Your own casket or urn. A funeral home can't refuse one bought elsewhere, or charge a fee for using it. No false claims. A funeral home can't say embalming is required by law when it isn't. It's rarely required by law, though some funeral homes require it for a public viewing. Cremation containers. Funeral homes offering direct cremation have to make an inexpensive alternative container available, rather than requiring a casket. What it doesn't cover The rule applies to funeral homes. Cemeteries, crematories that don't sell funeral services, and third-party sellers generally aren't covered, though some states have their own rules for them. If something seems wrong Complaints can be filed with the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov, and with the state board that licenses funeral directors. Bringing a friend who isn't grieving to the funeral home is common. They can ask about prices while the family focuses on the decisions.

t: Transportation and mileage charges: what to ask before you sign
pre: Getting from one place to another can add up quietly.
body: Several lines on a funeral bill are about moving the person or the family: from the place of death, to a service, to the cemetery or crematory. These charges are easy to miss until the final bill. Charges that often appear Transfer of remains: bringing the person from a home, hospital or care facility to the funeral home Hearse: transport to the service and to the cemetery Service car or van: carrying flowers, paperwork or equipment Family limousine: optional cars for the family Mileage: an extra charge per mile beyond a set distance Out-of-state transport: shipping or driving the person to another state for burial Questions families often ask Is transfer of remains included in a package, or listed separately? How many miles are included before mileage charges start, and what's the rate? Is there an after-hours or weekend fee for the first transfer? If the person died out of state, can a local funeral home there handle the transfer, and is that cheaper? Are any of these optional? Under the federal Funeral Rule, transfer of remains and the hearse each have to be listed with a price on the funeral home's General Price List, so the numbers can be compared before anything is signed. When someone dies far from home, families sometimes use two funeral homes: one near the place of death to handle the transfer, and one at home for the service. Asking both for prices can show which arrangement costs less.

t: Securing the home and car
pre: A quiet house and an unused car are both easy targets.
body: When someone lived alone, their home and car may sit empty for weeks after a death. Obituaries and funeral notices are public, and unfortunately some people watch them. A few simple steps can protect the house and what's in it. The home Locking doors and windows, and collecting spare keys from neighbors, cleaners or caregivers Changing locks if many people had keys Throwing out perishable food and checking that the stove, heaters and water are off Moving valuables, important papers and medications somewhere safe Keeping lights on a timer and lawn or snow taken care of so the house looks lived in Asking a neighbor to keep an eye on it during the funeral Insurance Many homeowners policies limit coverage once a house has been empty for a while, often after 30 or 60 days. Calling the insurer to explain the situation is common, and they can say what the policy requires. The car Keeping it in a garage or driveway, locked, with the keys somewhere safe Keeping the insurance active until the car is sold or transferred Not letting anyone drive it until the insurer confirms they're covered Executors usually aren't supposed to give away or sell belongings until they have legal authority. Securing things is fine; distributing them can wait.

t: Pausing and forwarding mail
pre: Mail is a map of every account. It also attracts identity thieves.
body: After a death, mail keeps arriving: bills, statements, renewals and junk. That mail is useful, because it shows which accounts exist. Left in an unattended mailbox, it can also be stolen and used for identity theft. Forwarding mail The US Postal Service lets the executor or estate administrator forward a deceased person's mail. This is usually done in person at the local post office, with proof of authority such as letters testamentary from the probate court. Rules and documents can vary, so checking with the local post office first is common. Holding mail for a short time For a short gap, such as the week of the funeral, a family member at the same address can request a USPS Hold Mail service online or at the post office. Reducing junk mail The Association of National Advertisers runs a Deceased Do Not Contact list through DMAchoice.org. Registering a name there can reduce marketing mail over time, though it doesn't stop bills or statements. What families often do with the mail Keeping every bill and statement in one folder Making a list of each company that writes, for closing accounts later Opening anything from a bank, insurer or government agency promptly A few months of mail is often the most complete list of accounts a family will ever get. Many executors wait at least a full year before stopping forwarding, so annual bills and tax forms arrive too.

t: Notifying Social Security
pre: Often the funeral home does it. A few things are still up to the family.
body: The Social Security Administration needs to know about a death to stop payments and check for survivor benefits. In most cases, the funeral home reports the death to Social Security, using the information the family gives them. Reporting it yourself If no funeral home is involved, or the family wants to make sure the death was reported, they can call Social Security at 1-800-772-1213, or visit a local office. The SSA doesn't accept death reports online. Having the person's Social Security number ready helps. Payments after a death Social Security pays benefits a month behind. A person isn't due a payment for the month they die, so a payment that arrives the following month usually has to be returned. If it was a direct deposit, the bank is usually asked to return it. Benefits the family may get A one-time death payment of $255, paid to a surviving spouse or child who meets certain requirements. It has to be applied for within 2 years. Monthly survivor benefits, for a widow or widower, children, or sometimes dependent parents, depending on the person's work record Survivor benefits aren't automatic in every case. Families usually need to apply by phone or at an office. Social Security shares death information with some other federal agencies, but not everyone. Medicare is usually updated automatically; banks, pensions and private insurers aren't.

t: Notifying an employer and claiming workplace benefits
pre: A job can leave behind more than a final paycheck.
body: If the person was working when they died, their employer usually has money and benefits to pay out. Some of these have deadlines, so families often contact HR within the first few weeks. What an employer may owe The final paycheck, and in some states, unused vacation pay. State laws vary. Group life insurance, often one or two times salary, sometimes with extra coverage the person bought Retirement accounts like a 401(k) or 403(b), which go to the named beneficiary A pension, if there is one, which may pay a survivor benefit Stock options, bonuses or commissions that were owed Health insurance for the family If the family was covered through the person's job, coverage usually ends soon after the death. When a covered employee dies, the federal COBRA law usually lets their spouse and dependents keep the same coverage for up to 36 months, though they pay the full cost. COBRA generally applies to employers with 20 or more employees, and many states have similar rules for smaller ones. Losing job-based coverage also allows the family to sign up for a marketplace plan at HealthCare.gov outside the usual enrollment period, usually within 60 days. What HR usually asks for A certified copy of the death certificate The beneficiary's details for each benefit Sometimes proof of the executor's authority Former employers can matter too. An old pension or a 401(k) left at a past job still pays out. The US Department of Labor's free Retirement Savings Lost and Found database can help find plans from former employers.

t: Notifying the credit bureaus to prevent identity theft
pre: A name and Social Security number can still be misused after death.
body: Identity thieves sometimes use the details of people who have died, because no one is watching the accounts. Telling the three credit bureaus about a death helps stop new credit being opened in the person's name. How it usually works Equifax, Experian and TransUnion each accept death notices, usually by mail. The family member or executor typically sends a letter with a copy of the death certificate, proof of their role (such as letters testamentary), and the person's full name, date of birth, Social Security number and last address. The bureau then marks the file as deceased. Social Security may eventually report the death, but it can take time and doesn't always reach every bureau. Many families contact all three directly. Checking the credit report The executor or a surviving spouse can usually request the person's credit report. It lists open credit cards and loans, which helps with closing accounts and spotting anything suspicious. Other steps families often take Leaving the person's age and date of birth out of a published obituary Shredding mail with account numbers Closing credit cards rather than leaving them open Reporting any suspicious activity at IdentityTheft.gov Each bureau's mailing address and requirements change from time to time. Searching "[bureau name] report a deceased person" usually finds the current process.

t: Freezing vs. closing bank accounts
pre: Some accounts stop, some keep going, and some pass straight to someone else.
body: When a bank learns about a death, what happens next depends on how the account is set up. Many families are surprised to find a bank account frozen just when bills need paying. How the account is set up What usually happens In one person's name only, no beneficiary Frozen. Only the executor can access it, usually after probate or with a small-estate affidavit. Joint account with right of survivorship Passes to the other owner, who can usually keep using it Payable-on-death (POD) beneficiary Paid to the beneficiary once they show a death certificate and ID Held in a living trust Managed by the successor trustee What "frozen" usually means A frozen account can't be used for new withdrawals, checks or card payments. Automatic payments from it may stop. Deposits may still come in, but some, like Social Security payments for the month after the death, are usually pulled back. Moving the money Executors often open an estate bank account in the estate's name. Money from frozen accounts goes there, and the estate's bills are paid from it. Most banks require letters testamentary and a tax ID number for the estate. Small estates Many states have a simpler process for smaller estates, often called a small-estate affidavit. The limits vary widely by state. Using a debit card or writing checks from someone's account after they die, even to pay their bills, can cause legal trouble for whoever does it. Many families wait until the executor has authority.

t: Cremation: what it costs and what the options are
pre: Simpler and usually cheaper than burial, with more choices than people expect.
body: Cremation is now chosen by more US families than burial, and cost is one of the most common reasons. It also leaves more room for choices about when and how to hold a service. The main options Option What it usually includes Relative cost Direct cremation Transfer, the cremation itself, a basic container and the return of ashes. No viewing or service beforehand. Lowest Cremation with a memorial service Direct cremation, plus a service later with or without the ashes present Low to moderate Cremation with a viewing or funeral first Embalming, a rental or purchased casket, a viewing or service, then cremation Closer to a traditional funeral According to the National Funeral Directors Association, the national median cost of a funeral with viewing and cremation was $6,280 in 2023. Direct cremation is usually far less, and prices vary a lot by region and provider. What families often ask about Whether the quoted price includes the death certificate, the cremation permit and the medical examiner's fee, which some areas charge Whether a casket is needed. It isn't. Under the federal Funeral Rule, a funeral home offering direct cremation has to make a simple alternative container available. How long it takes. Many states require a waiting period, often 24 to 48 hours, before cremation can happen. Whether the urn has to come from the provider. It doesn't. Any container can be used. What people do with the ashes Keeping them at home Burying them in a cemetery plot or a niche in a columbarium Scattering them somewhere meaningful. Rules for public land, parks and water vary, and scattering at sea is covered by federal rules. Dividing them among family members There's no deadline for deciding what to do with the ashes. Many families wait months, or until a meaningful date.

t: Do you need a funeral home? Other options families use
pre: In most states, a funeral home is a choice, not a requirement.
body: Many people assume a funeral home is legally required after a death. In most states it isn't. Families can usually handle the arrangements themselves, or use a provider that offers only the parts they need. A few states do require a licensed funeral director for certain steps, such as filing the death certificate or moving the body. Options families use Direct cremation providers. Many work mostly online or by phone and handle only the transfer, paperwork and cremation, often for much less than a full-service funeral home. Body donation. Medical schools and some programs accept donated bodies for education and research. Many cover transport and cremation, and return the ashes later. Most require registration in advance, and they can decline a donation. Home funerals. The family cares for the person at home for a day or two and handles the paperwork themselves, sometimes with help from a home funeral guide. State rules on permits and timing apply. Green or natural burial. No embalming, a simple shroud or biodegradable casket, in a natural burial ground or a section of a conventional cemetery. Memorial service only. A simple cremation or burial first, then a gathering later, wherever and whenever the family likes. Things to know A death certificate still has to be filed, and a permit is usually needed to move or cremate a body. Families handling it themselves deal with these directly. If the death is unexpected, a medical examiner or coroner may need to be involved first. Cemeteries can set their own rules, such as requiring a burial vault, even if state law doesn't. Funeral consumer groups, such as the nonprofit Funeral Consumers Alliance, publish state-by-state guides on what families can do themselves.

t: Choosing a funeral home, and what to know before you call
pre: Ten minutes of preparation can change the whole conversation.
body: The first call to a funeral home often happens within hours of a death, when families are exhausted and in shock. Knowing a few things beforehand makes it easier to compare options and decide calmly. What families often decide or gather first Burial or cremation, if the person said what they wanted A rough budget, even a range Whether there's a prepaid funeral plan, and with which funeral home Whether the person was a veteran, since burial benefits may apply Any religious or cultural needs, such as timing or washing Whether there's life insurance that might help with costs Comparing funeral homes Under the federal Funeral Rule, funeral homes have to give prices over the phone and provide an itemized price list in person. Many families call two or three. Prices for the same service can differ by thousands of dollars in the same town. Questions families often ask What is the basic services fee, and what does it cover? What does direct cremation or direct burial cost, all in? Can we bring our own casket or urn? Is embalming required for what we're planning, and why? What's included in this package, and can we remove items? Common sales pressure Most funeral directors are honest and caring. Still, the FTC created the Funeral Rule because families were often overcharged at a vulnerable time. Situations families commonly report include: Being told a more expensive option is what the person "deserves" Packages that include services the family didn't ask for "Protective" or sealed caskets presented as preserving the body. No casket does that indefinitely. Being told embalming is required by law when it usually isn't Pressure to decide quickly It's okay to say "We need to think about it" and call back. Many families bring a friend who isn't grieving to help ask questions.

t: When someone dies abroad
pre: The US embassy can help, but it can't pay for anything.
body: When a US citizen dies in another country, the nearest US embassy or consulate is usually involved. Local laws, languages and costs can make the next steps complicated, so knowing who does what helps. What the US government usually does Tells the next of kin, if local authorities haven't already Explains the options and local requirements for burial, cremation or bringing the person home Provides a list of local funeral homes and English-speaking lawyers Issues a Consular Report of Death of a US Citizen Abroad, which is used in US legal matters like probate and insurance Helps the family send money for costs The embassy can't pay for funeral costs or bringing the person home. Those are the family's responsibility. The main options Bringing the person home. This can be expensive, and it involves international transport, embalming and paperwork from both countries. Cremation abroad, then bringing the ashes home. Usually far cheaper and simpler, where local law and religion allow it. Burial in the country where they died. Some families choose this, especially if the person lived there. Insurance that can help Some travel insurance policies cover repatriation, meaning bringing someone home after a death. Credit cards used to book the trip sometimes include travel coverage too. Most US health insurance and Medicare don't cover it. Who to call Families in the US can call the State Department's Office of Overseas Citizens Services at 1-888-407-4747. From overseas, the number is +1-202-501-4444. A death abroad may need a certified, translated copy of the local death certificate, as well as the Consular Report of Death. Asking the embassy for several copies of the report is common.

t: Claiming life insurance, step by step
pre: Usually one form, one death certificate, and a few weeks.
body: Life insurance is often the fastest money to reach a family after a death, because it usually goes straight to the named beneficiary without probate. The beneficiary, not the executor, usually starts the claim. How a claim usually works Finding the policy. The insurer's name and policy number are the main things needed. Both are usually on the first page of the policy, on annual statements, or in the insurer's app. Contacting the insurer. Most have a claims phone line or online form. Employers handle claims for work policies through HR. Filling in the claim form. It asks for the beneficiary's details and how they'd like to be paid. Sending a certified copy of the death certificate. Some insurers accept a photocopy; others want a certified one. Waiting for review. Many claims are paid within a few weeks once the paperwork is complete. Ways the money is usually paid A lump sum, by check or direct deposit Installments over time A retained asset account, where the insurer holds the money and gives the beneficiary a checkbook. It's worth reading the terms, since it may pay less interest than a regular bank. When claims take longer The death happened within the first two years of the policy. State insurance laws generally allow insurers to review the application more closely during this period, often called the contestability period. Nearly every state has a version of this rule. The cause of death is still being determined The beneficiary has died, is a minor or isn't clear Life insurance payouts to a beneficiary generally aren't counted as taxable income under federal rules, though interest earned on the payout can be.

t: Cancelling subscriptions (Netflix, gym and the rest)
pre: The small charges add up, and some are hard to find.
body: Subscriptions often keep charging long after someone dies. Many are small, so they're easy to miss, and they can go on for months on a card nobody is watching. Where to find them Credit card and bank statements: recurring charges each month or year The person's email: receipts, renewal notices and "your plan has been renewed" messages Apple or Google subscriptions on their phone PayPal or Amazon account settings Paper mail: magazines, memberships and charities How cancelling usually works Many services can be cancelled by logging into the account. Without the login, most companies will cancel with a phone call or online form, a copy of the death certificate and proof of the caller's role. Some ask for less.
