Gyms and some memberships have contracts. Many will end them early after a death, but it's worth asking. Ones that may be worth keeping for a bit Cloud storage holding photos or documents, until they're downloaded Email, until accounts and bills are sorted Home security, if the house is empty Closing the credit card the subscriptions charge to will stop most of them, but not all, and some keep trying for months. Cancelling each one directly avoids surprises.

t: Probate basics: what it is and when it's needed
pre: The court process for settling an estate, and when families can skip it.
body: Probate is the court-supervised process of settling someone's estate after they die. It confirms who's in charge, pays debts and taxes, and transfers what's left to the people who should get it. What usually happens in probate Someone files the will, if there is one, with the local probate court. The court appoints an executor (named in the will) or an administrator (if there's no will). The executor finds and values the person's assets. Creditors are notified and given a set time to make claims. Debts, final bills and taxes are paid. What's left is distributed, and the court closes the estate. Simple probate cases often take several months to a year. Contested or complicated estates can take longer. What usually skips probate Accounts with a named beneficiary, like life insurance, retirement accounts, and POD or TOD accounts Jointly owned property with right of survivorship Assets held in a living trust Small estates Most states have a simpler process for smaller estates, such as a small-estate affidavit or summary probate. The dollar limits and rules vary widely by state. Searching "[your state] small estate affidavit" shows whether a simpler process is available and what the limit is.

t: What an executor actually does
pre: A to-do list that can stretch over months, not days.
body: An executor is the person named in a will to settle the estate. If there's no will, a court appoints someone, usually called an administrator, to do the same job. It's a big responsibility, but most of it is paperwork and patience. The usual stages First weeks Finding the will, getting certified death certificates, securing the home and belongings, and notifying close contacts First months Filing for probate if needed, getting letters testamentary, opening an estate bank account, getting a tax ID for the estate, and notifying banks, creditors and agencies Middle months Listing and valuing assets, paying valid debts and bills, managing property, and keeping careful records Final stage Filing final tax returns, distributing what's left to beneficiaries, and closing the estate Duties executors usually have Acting in the best interest of the estate and beneficiaries, not themselves Keeping estate money separate from their own Keeping records of everything they receive and pay Not distributing anything until debts and taxes are handled Getting help Executors can usually pay for a lawyer or accountant from the estate's money. Many states also allow executors to be paid a fee, though many family members decline it. Being named executor doesn't mean someone has to do it. They can decline, and the court will appoint someone else.

t: Retitling a house or car
pre: Ownership has to move into someone's name. How depends on how it was held.
body: After a death, houses and cars still list the person as owner. Until the title is changed, they usually can't be sold, refinanced or properly insured by someone else. The process depends on how the property was owned. The house How it was owned What usually happens Joint tenancy with right of survivorship The surviving owner records a death certificate and sometimes an affidavit with the county recorder. Transfer-on-death deed (available in some states) The beneficiary records the death certificate and a form with the county recorder. Held in a living trust The successor trustee transfers or sells it under the trust's terms. In the person's name only Usually goes through probate. The executor transfers it with a new deed once the court allows. The car Most state DMVs have a process for transferring a vehicle after the owner dies. It usually needs the title, a death certificate, and proof of who inherits it, such as letters testamentary, a small-estate affidavit or a transfer-on-death title. Some states allow a simple affidavit for cars below a certain value. Loans If there's a mortgage or car loan, it stays with the property. Payments are still due, and whoever inherits usually keeps up the payments, refinances, pays off the loan or sells. Federal law generally lets a relative who inherits a home keep the existing mortgage rather than having to pay it off right away. Recording fees and forms vary by county and state. The county recorder's website and the state DMV site usually list exactly what they need.

t: Filing a final tax return for someone who died
pre: One more year of taxes, usually filed by the executor or spouse.
body: When someone dies, a final federal income tax return is usually due for the year of their death, covering income from January 1 to the date they died. A surviving spouse or the executor typically files it. The final return It's filed on the regular Form 1040, usually by the normal April deadline of the following year. A surviving spouse can usually still file a joint return for the year of death. "Deceased" and the date of death are written at the top of the form. If there's a refund and no surviving spouse filing jointly, the IRS may need Form 1310. An estate return may also be needed After the death, the estate itself can earn income, such as interest, dividends or rent. If the estate has $600 or more in gross income in a year, the executor usually files Form 1041, a separate income tax return for the estate. The federal estate tax Very few estates owe federal estate tax, because it only applies to estates above a high threshold that changes each year. Some states have their own estate or inheritance taxes with lower thresholds. Letting the IRS know who's in charge Executors often file Form 56 to tell the IRS they're handling the person's tax matters, so the IRS sends notices to them. Free help is available. The IRS Volunteer Income Tax Assistance (VITA) program helps people who qualify, and many tax preparers handle final returns.

t: What happens to debt when someone dies
pre: Debt usually stays with the estate, not the family.
body: One of the most common worries after a death is whether the family has to pay the person's debts. In most cases they don't personally owe them. Debts are paid from the estate, the money and property the person left. How it usually works The executor uses estate money to pay valid debts before anything goes to heirs. If the estate runs out of money, most remaining debts usually go unpaid. State law sets the order debts are paid in. Funeral costs, estate expenses and taxes usually come first. When someone else may owe it They co-signed the loan or were a joint account holder They live in a community-property state, where a spouse may be responsible for some debts State law makes a spouse responsible for certain debts, such as some medical bills What usually doesn't go to creditors Life insurance and retirement accounts paid to a named beneficiary usually aren't part of the estate, so creditors generally can't claim them. Debt collectors Collectors can contact the executor. Under federal rules, they can't say or suggest that family members are personally responsible when they aren't. Families can report problems to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. Federal student loans are discharged when the borrower dies. Private loans and other debts follow the rules above.

t: Belongings: there's no need to rush
pre: The clothes, the dishes, the car in the garage. They can wait.
body: Many families feel pressure to sort through belongings quickly, often from well-meaning relatives, a lease ending or the sheer weight of it. Unless there's a deadline, there's usually no reason to rush. Why waiting often helps Grief makes decisions harder. Things given away in the first weeks are sometimes regretted later. The executor usually needs to list valuable items before anything is distributed. Papers mixed in with belongings, like statements, policies and old tax returns, can matter for settling the estate. When there is a deadline A rental lease ending. Many landlords will work with families on timing. A care facility needing the room Selling the house Ways families make it easier Starting with one small area, like a drawer or a closet Setting aside anything with paperwork to go through later Taking photos of things before letting them go Asking each family member for one or two items that matter most Using a "maybe" box for things nobody can decide on yet If there's a written "who gets what" list, it's worth finding before sorting begins. In some states it can be legally binding if the will refers to it, and even where it isn't, families often follow it.

t: The first month: what can wait
pre: A shorter list than it feels like.
body: In the first month after a death, it can feel like everything is urgent. A few things are. Most things can wait weeks or months without causing problems. What usually can't wait Funeral or cremation arrangements Securing the home, car and any pets Ordering death certificates Finding the will Keeping up mortgage, rent, insurance and utility payments Telling Social Security, if the funeral home hasn't What can usually wait a few weeks Filing for probate Closing bank accounts Claiming life insurance, though it's often worth starting early Cancelling subscriptions Notifying the credit bureaus What can usually wait months Sorting and giving away belongings Selling the house or car Closing email and social media accounts Filing the final tax return, usually due in April of the following year Deciding what to do with the ashes The phone line is worth keeping active for a while. It's often what unlocks the person's other accounts. Banks and email often text a code to that number before they let anyone in, so many families keep it running for 3 to 6 months.

t: Looking after yourself while you handle it all
pre: The paperwork matters. So do you.
body: Handling someone's affairs after they die often falls on one person, at the same time they're grieving. Many people who've done it say they wish someone had told them to slow down and ask for help. Things people often find helpful Keeping a single notebook or document for every call, account and reference number Doing one or two tasks a day rather than trying to finish everything at once Saying yes when people offer help, and giving them a specific task, like returning calls, picking up mail or making meals Taking breaks from paperwork entirely, especially on hard days like birthdays and holidays Grief is not a schedule There's no right way or right timeline to grieve. Some people feel numb for weeks, some are fine and then aren't. Many find it helps to talk with others who've been through it. Where people find support Hospice organizations, many of which offer free bereavement support to families, even if the person wasn't in hospice care Grief support groups through hospitals, places of worship or community centers Employee assistance programs (EAPs) through work, which often include free counseling sessions A doctor or therapist, especially if grief is affecting sleep, eating or daily life If you're struggling or having thoughts of harming yourself, you can call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, any time. Many employers offer bereavement leave. It's worth asking HR, even if you think you don't qualify.

t: How to close a Chase account for someone who died
pre: Chase has a dedicated process, and much of it can start online.
body: Chase, like most large banks, has a team that handles accounts after a customer dies. The steps depend on how the account was set up and who is contacting the bank. How it usually starts Chase's website has a section for reporting a customer's death, where a family member or executor can start the process online or find the right phone number. Families can also visit a branch. Searching "Chase bereavement" or "Chase report a death" usually finds the current page. What Chase typically asks for The customer's full name and Social Security number A death certificate The caller's own ID Proof of authority if they're the executor, such as letters testamentary or a small-estate affidavit, depending on the state What usually happens next How the account was held What usually happens Joint account The surviving owner usually keeps the account and can remove the deceased person's name Payable-on-death beneficiary The beneficiary receives the funds after showing the death certificate and ID Individual account, no beneficiary The account is frozen and the funds go to the executor, usually into an estate account Credit cards and loans Chase credit cards, car loans and mortgages are handled separately from bank accounts. The same bereavement team can usually point families to each one. Requirements change, and they can vary by state and account type. Asking Chase for a written list of what they need before sending anything saves a second trip.

t: Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Citi: what each one asks for
pre: The big banks ask for similar things, with small differences.
body: Most large US banks follow a similar process after a customer dies. Each has a bereavement or estate services team, a page on its website, and a list of documents it needs. What most of them ask for The customer's full legal name and Social Security number A death certificate, often a certified copy The ID of the person contacting them Proof of authority for an executor or administrator, such as letters testamentary, letters of administration or a small-estate affidavit For a payable-on-death beneficiary, their ID and the death certificate How each one usually starts Bank of America: an online form for reporting a death, plus a phone line and branches Wells Fargo: an online form or a call to its estate services team, and branches can help Citi: searching "Citi deceased customer" finds its current steps and phone number Searching "[bank name] report a death" or "[bank name] estate services" usually finds the current page and phone number. Differences families sometimes notice Whether a certified death certificate is required, or a photocopy is enough Whether documents can be uploaded online or must be mailed or brought in How long the process takes, often a few weeks Keeping a list of each bank, the date of each call, who was spoken to and any reference number makes follow-up calls much faster.

t: How to cancel a credit card for someone who died
pre: The card closes. The balance goes to the estate.
body: Credit cards don't pass on to family members. After a death, card companies close the account and the balance becomes a debt of the estate, paid from the person's money and property before anything goes to heirs. How it usually works Contacting each card company. Most have a phone line or online form for reporting a death. Providing the death certificate and the executor's details. Asking the company to close the account and send a final statement to the executor. Stopping any automatic payments that charged to the card. Who owes the balance Role on the card Usually responsible for the balance? Account holder Yes, through their estate Joint account holder Yes, personally Authorized user No. They usually just stop using the card. In community-property states, a surviving spouse may be responsible for some debts even if they weren't on the card. Rules vary. Things families commonly do Not using the card after the death, even to pay the person's bills Destroying the cards once the accounts are closed Checking the credit report for cards nobody knew about Under federal rules, card companies can't tell family members they have to pay a debt they don't legally owe. Families can report problems to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

t: Store cards and buy-now-pay-later accounts
pre: The small accounts that are easy to forget.
body: Store credit cards and buy-now-pay-later plans, like Affirm, Klarna and Afterpay, are often missed after a death. They may not show up in the same places as a regular credit card, and some only send emails. Where they usually show up The credit report. Store cards almost always appear. Buy-now-pay-later plans increasingly do, but not always. Email receipts and payment reminders Bank and credit card statements, as automatic payments Apps on the person's phone How closing them usually works Store cards work like other credit cards: the company is told about the death, the account is closed, and the balance becomes a debt of the estate. Buy-now-pay-later companies usually have a support form or email for reporting a death, and follow a similar process. Who owes the balance As with other debts, the estate usually pays. Family members generally don't owe it unless they co-signed or shared the account. Automatic payments for these plans often come from a debit card. If the bank account is frozen, payments may fail, so telling the company early can prevent late fees from piling up on the estate.

t: Different ways to cash out an account
pre: Checks, transfers, and accounts that pass straight to someone.
body: Once a bank or brokerage agrees who should receive an account's money, there are usually a few ways to get it there. The options depend on who's receiving it and what kind of account it is. Method How it works Often used for Check The bank mails a check, usually to the executor or beneficiary Smaller balances, or when someone doesn't bank with the same institution Transfer to an estate account Money moves into a bank account opened in the estate's name Accounts with no beneficiary, settled through probate Transfer to the beneficiary's account Money moves straight to the beneficiary's own account Payable-on-death and transfer-on-death accounts Transfer in kind Investments move as they are, without being sold Brokerage accounts, to avoid selling and possible taxes Retirement accounts are different Inherited IRAs and 401(k)s have their own rules. Beneficiaries often have the choice of moving the money into an inherited IRA rather than cashing it out, which can spread out the taxes. The rules depend on who the beneficiary is and when the person died. Taxes Cash in a bank account usually isn't taxable income to the person who inherits it. Interest earned after the death can be. Withdrawals from traditional retirement accounts usually are taxable. Brokerage investments usually get a new cost basis when the owner dies, often their value on the date of death. That can lower taxes when they're eventually sold.

t: Opening an estate bank account
pre: One account for everything the estate pays and receives.
body: An estate bank account is opened in the name of the person's estate, and managed by the executor. It keeps the estate's money separate from everyone else's, which makes paying bills and keeping records much easier. What banks usually ask for Letters testamentary or letters of administration from the probate court A tax ID number for the estate, called an EIN A death certificate The executor's own ID Getting an EIN The IRS issues EINs for free, and many executors get one online in a few minutes at irs.gov. The estate uses it instead of the person's Social Security number. What usually goes in and out In Out Money from closed bank accounts Funeral costs, if not already paid Final paychecks and refunds Mortgage, utilities and insurance on the home Proceeds from selling property Valid debts and final bills Interest and dividends Taxes, legal fees, and final distributions to heirs Keeping records Courts and beneficiaries can ask the executor to show what came in and what went out. Paying everything from one account makes that much simpler. Executors usually avoid paying estate bills from their own accounts. If they do, keeping receipts helps them get repaid from the estate later.

t: Utilities: transfer or cancel
pre: Some need to keep running for months.
body: Utilities are among the few bills that usually need to keep being paid after a death, at least while the home is still being cared for or sold. Turning off power or water too early can lead to frozen pipes, mold or an insurance problem. Utilities families usually keep running Electricity and gas, especially for heating and cooling Water and sewer Trash collection Home security or alarm monitoring, if the house is empty Ones that can often be cancelled sooner Cable or satellite TV Streaming services A landline, if the cell phone is being kept Internet, unless a smart thermostat or camera needs it Transferring to someone else If a family member is moving in or taking over the home, most utility companies will transfer the account into their name with a phone call, the account number and sometimes a death certificate. Deposits and refunds Some utility companies hold a deposit. When the account is closed, any deposit or credit balance usually goes to the estate. Recent utility bills are often the quickest way to find each company and account number.

t: Closing an email account (Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo)
pre: Email is often the last account to close, for good reason.
body: Email accounts often hold the most useful information after a death: bills, statements, receipts and messages from companies. Many families keep an account open until other accounts are settled, if they can get into it. If the family has the password Signing in with the person's password may be possible, but the major providers' terms of service usually prohibit using someone else's account, and two-factor codes may still go to the person's phone. Some families keep the account open just long enough to download what they need. How the major providers usually handle it Gmail (Google): Google has a request form for a deceased user's account. Family members can ask to close the account, and in some cases request some of its data. If the person set up Inactive Account Manager, their chosen contacts may already have access. Outlook (Microsoft): Microsoft accounts usually close automatically after a period of inactivity. Microsoft generally doesn't give family access to an account's contents without a subpoena or court order. Yahoo: Yahoo has a process to close a deceased user's account. Under its terms, it generally doesn't give access to the account's contents. Searching "[provider] deceased user" usually finds the current form. What providers usually ask for A death certificate The requester's ID Sometimes proof of the requester's role, or a court order for access to content Because access is often limited after a death, settings like Google Inactive Account Manager, set up in advance, are the most reliable way to pass on email and files.

t: PayPal, Venmo and Cash App after a death
pre: Money can sit in these accounts, and they don't close themselves.
body: Payment apps can hold a balance, and they're easy to forget because they don't send paper statements. Each has its own process after an account holder dies. How each one usually handles it PayPal: the executor or estate administrator, not other family members, can ask PayPal to close the account through its help center. Once the death is verified, the account is usually closed and any balance is paid to the estate, often by check. Venmo: owned by PayPal, Venmo has a similar process through its support team. Any balance usually goes to the estate. Cash App: Cash App's support handles deceased accounts. Families usually contact support through the app or website. Searching "[app name] deceased account" usually finds the current process. What they usually ask for A death certificate The executor's ID Proof of authority, such as letters testamentary Things families commonly check Any balance sitting in the account Linked bank accounts and cards, which may need updating Automatic payments or subscriptions paid through the app Bitcoin or stocks held in Cash App, which may be handled separately from the cash balance Payment app balances usually aren't FDIC-insured the way bank deposits are. According to the CFPB, some may be covered by pass-through insurance when the app holds the money at a partner bank, for example with an app debit card or direct deposit. Crypto held in an app isn't covered. Moving the balance to the estate account sooner rather than later is common.

t: Keeping a closing log
pre: One page that saves dozens of repeat phone calls.
body: Closing accounts after a death means a lot of calls, forms and follow-ups, often spread over months. A simple log of every contact helps keep track of what's done, what's waiting, and what was promised. What a log usually includes Column Example Company Chase checking Account (last 4) …4821 Date contacted Oct 14 How Phone, branch, online form Who you spoke to Maria, bereavement team Reference number CB-20391 What they need Certified death certificate, letters testamentary Status Waiting on check to estate account Ways families keep it A notebook kept by the phone A spreadsheet that others in the family can see A page in the binder, next to the account list Why it helps It avoids sending the same documents twice It's easy to hand off if someone else takes over It shows the executor's work if beneficiaries or a court ask It makes it clear when something has stalled and needs a follow-up Writing the date and the name of the person spoken to on every call is the single most useful habit. Many companies can look up a call by those two details.
